title: Shadow Length Calculator: Height and Sun
description: Compute shadow length from object height and sun angle with the Shadow Length Calculator — solar-noon extremes and design uses included. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 10-metre building in New York casts a noon shadow of just 3.11 metres at the June solstice — and 20.62 metres in December, which is why winter sun feels rationed.
quick_answer: The Shadow Length Calculator works out how long a shadow an object casts, from its height and the Sun's altitude — length equals height divided by the tangent of the sun angle. Enter the height and read the shadow — the arithmetic behind sundials, gardens and solar siting.

popular_table.note: Assumes flat ground and a vertical object; slopes stretch or shrink the real shadow — the calculator's flat-ground assumption is stated, not hidden.

faq: Shadow = height ÷ tan(sun altitude). At 45° the shadow equals the height; below that it grows fast, which the ratio table makes visceral.
Where does the sun angle come from?
From place, date and time via the solar-position math — or type an altitude directly if you measured one. The Sun Altitude Calculator is the dedicated source.
Morning and evening shadows point where?
Opposite the Sun's azimuth: morning shadows point west-ish, evening east-ish, swinging with the season — direction is the Sun Azimuth Calculator's department.
Can it work backwards (shadow to height)?
Yes — measure a shadow and the Sun's altitude and the same triangle returns the object's height: the surveyor's oldest trick.
Slopes change everything: downhill shadows stretch, uphill shrink. The calculator assumes flat ground and says so; treat sloped results as first approximations.
The triangle gives the shadow's core (umbra) length; leafy canopies feather the edge. For siting decisions the core length is the conservative number.
Infinite in the limit — as altitude approaches zero the shadow leaves the map. Practically, buildings and terrain end it first.
